The Big Data Pipeline
Multi-gigabyte AIS CSV files streamed row-by-row via Python generators, cleaned, chunked, and processed in parallel across CPU workers — without ever loading the full file into memory
📡
Streaming Process
  • Reads header once → O(1) column lookup
  • Yields 7 fields from ~50 columns per row
  • Chains 2 CSV files into one continuous stream
  • Assigns global chunk_id for ordered merging
  • 10 GB file uses same RAM as one chunk

⚙️
Parallel Workers
  • Pool.imap_unordered — N cores in parallel
  • parser.py cleans inside each worker: Class A only, 9-digit MMSI, valid coords
  • Groups by MMSI, sorts by timestamp
  • Downsamples to 5-min for anomalies A & C
  • Detects A, B, C, D1, D2 per chunk

chunk results
out-of-order
🔗
Merge Process
  • Buffers results, reassembles by chunk_id
  • Compares boundary: last of chunk N vs first of N+1
  • Catches anomalies spanning chunk boundaries
  • A & C use sampled records; D uses full-res
  • D1 and D2 tracked separately

Scoring & Output
  • Aggregates all events per vessel
  • Computes DFSI score for every MMSI
  • Ranks vessels by suspicion descending
  • Writes dfsi_results.csv + map CSVs
  • MemoryMonitor logs RAM throughout

Anomaly Detection Engine
Four suspicious behaviours detected in rules.py — every consecutive AIS ping pair checked against all rules simultaneously
🌑
ANOMALY A
Going Dark
Vessel disables AIS transponder while continuing to move — conceals route, port calls, and cargo activity from authorities and tracking systems.
gap > 4 hours distance > 1 km haversine dist
  • Detected by detect_going_dark() in rules.py
  • Stationary vessels excluded — movement required
  • Runs on 5-min downsampled records
  • DFSI contribution: max_gap_hours / 2

📈 Memory & Runtime Benchmarks

Heatmap overview, speedup scaling, runtime behaviour, and Amdahl's Law fit across chunk sizes and worker counts

w4 benchmark · 250K & 100K chunks
Peak process memory (MB) and runtime (s) across all configurations — Memory scales with chunk size (rows), not worker count (columns) — values hold steady across 1–4 workers at any given chunk size. Runtime halves at 2 workers and barely changes beyond that.
Speedup vs number of workers across chunk sizes — All chunk sizes jump from 1.0× to ~1.8× at 2 workers then plateau. Larger chunks (250K–1000K) reach marginally higher speedup than 100K chunks, which suffer slightly more from IPC overhead.
Runtime vs chunk size for 1–4 workers — Single-worker runtime sits at 400–420 seconds across all chunk sizes. All multi-worker configurations (2–4) cluster tightly at 220–240 seconds with only a slight upward drift at larger chunks, confirming chunk size has minimal impact once parallelism is active.
Amdahl's Law fit — chunk size 250K (P = 67.8% parallel) — The measured speedup plateaus at ~1.8× beyond 2 workers, closely matching the Amdahl model. With 67.8% of the workload parallelisable, the remaining 32.2% — streaming ingestion and sequential merge logic — caps the theoretical maximum speedup at ~3.1×.

💻 Worker Memory Profiles

Peak memory scaling, per-worker footprints, and system RSS breakdown at 250K and 100K chunk sizes

w4 benchmark · 250K & 100K chunks
Peak worker memory vs chunk size (1–4 workers) — Memory grows linearly with chunk size across all worker counts. At 1000K rows, 4 workers reach ~1,600 MB — chunk size, not worker count, is the dominant driver of per-process memory demand.
Per-worker memory distribution — 4 workers, 250K chunk — All four workers cycle rapidly between 150 and 270 MB with nearly identical footprints. The tight clustering confirms balanced load distribution and no memory divergence between workers.
System-wide RSS timeline — 4 workers, 250K chunk — Workers RSS (orange) stabilises near 1,000 MB while the main process (blue) holds steady at ~300 MB. Total RSS (green) peaks around 1,400 MB then drops sharply when all processing finishes.
Per-worker memory distribution — 4 workers, 100K chunk — Halving the chunk size cuts per-worker memory to 140–160 MB, roughly half the 250K footprint. Workers still track identically, and the faster chunk cycling is visible in the tighter fluctuation pattern.
What We Found
pipeline design · results · performance
🏗️ Pipeline Design
Built to run on one machine, not a cluster
  • The pipeline runs on a single node using streaming input and incremental merging. It handles large AIS datasets without needing distributed infrastructure.
  • Multiprocessing is used within one machine to share the workload across workers while keeping everything under one roof.
🧠 Memory Strategy
Controlled parallelism, not raw power
  • The focus was on keeping memory use predictable rather than throwing more workers at the problem. Controlled parallelism means we can scale safely without unexpected spikes.
  • We avoided distributed execution on purpose — the goal was to prove the pipeline works efficiently on standard hardware first.
💻 In-Memory Processing
No temp files, everything stays in RAM
  • Intermediate results are never written to disk. All chunk outputs get merged in memory, so there are no leftover partial files to manage or clean up.
  • This keeps the code simpler and avoids the disk read-write cycles that slow down many data pipelines, especially with large datasets.
⚡ I/O Overhead
Skipping disk writes has a trade-off
  • By keeping everything in memory we cut down on I/O time, which is a real win for pipeline speed. The trade-off is higher memory pressure when chunk sizes grow large.
  • This trade-off shows up clearly in the benchmarks — at higher worker counts the memory bus becomes the real bottleneck, not CPU speed.
🚨 Detection Results
Two anomaly types found in the data
  • Out of five anomaly types the pipeline can detect, the visualizations confirmed two in this dataset: A (going dark) and D1 (cloning / simultaneous position spoofing).
  • The absence of C, D2 and B events is itself a finding — it means no cargo flag changes, no physically impossible relocations at sea, and no obvious loitering in the data.
📈 Parallelism Gains
Two workers is where the gains really show up
  • Going from 1 to 2 workers gives a strong speedup. Past that point adding more workers does not help much because the system hits its memory bandwidth ceiling instead.
  • It is not a CPU problem — the cores are available. The issue is that all workers share the same memory bus, and that bus gets saturated before the cores do.
⚖️ Optimal Configuration
2 workers + 250K rows is the practical sweet spot
  • 250K rows per chunk gives the best speed-to-memory ratio. Workers split the load evenly and memory stays within reasonable bounds for the whole run.
  • Since roughly a third of the work must run sequentially during merging, two workers with 250K chunks is the point where returns stop being worth the extra RAM cost.
🖥️ Hardware Note
Numbers are tied to this specific machine
  • All benchmarks ran on an i7-12700H with 16 GB DDR5 RAM. The exact numbers — speedup ceiling, optimal chunk size, memory per worker — reflect that setup specifically.
  • A machine with faster RAM or more cores could push the parallelism ceiling higher. The patterns we found should hold, but the exact thresholds will shift.
